newsitem.title: CYPRUS: U.S. envoy starts talks to defuse Cyprus tension.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy starts talks to defuse Cyprus tension.

text.p: A U.S. envoy starts contacts in Cyprus on Monday amid renewed tension with Turkey over Cypriot government plans to deploy Russian missiles on the divided island.

The United States, which has voiced concern at the Cypriot government's decision to purchase the missiles and threats by Turkey to retaliate with a military strike, has dispatched State Department official Carey Cavanaugh to the island to try to take the sting out of the row.
Turkey threatened military action several times last week to stop the deployment of the S-300 anti-aircraft missiles, which the Cypriot government said last week it was buying from Russia.

On Monday morning, Cavanaugh is due to meet Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides before travelling north across the ceasefire line dividing the island for talks with Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.

Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded northern Cyprus after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece. Turkey has around 30,000 troops in the northern third of Cyprus, which has declared a Turkish Cypriot state that is only recognised by Ankara.
Cavanaugh, who arrived on Sunday night, said he had "clear ideas" on how to resolve the tension, but he avoided comment on whether he would ask the Cypriot government to cancel the deal.
"I am going to discuss the missile deal and lay out the concerns we have and the problems that it poses for our diplomatic efforts," he said.
"I think it should be understood that that deal in many ways represents a setback to efforts the international community is trying to achieve on Cyprus."
Cavanaugh was equally critical of threats from Turkey, which occupies a third of the island.
"There can be no justification for military action. No aggressive action here can be justified in any form," he added.

The Turkish Cypriot administration in the northern part of the island also threatened to move people into Varosha, a now empty tourist resort once mainly owned by Greek Cypriots but now in occupied northern Cyprus.

The Cypriot government has refused to back down on the deal, saying the missiles are necessary for defensive purposes in the majority Greek Cypriot populated southern part of the island the event of an air raid by Turkey.
